passage: In most economic transactions, both buyers and sellers expect prices to remain relatively stable over short periods. However, in certain markets—most notably airlines, hotels, and ride-sharing platforms—companies rely on dynamic pricing, adjusting rates in real time based on fluctuating demand and available supply. When a sudden rainstorm hits a city or a major concert ends, ride-sharing algorithms immediately raise fares to reflect the spike in requests. Economists argue that surge pricing performs an essential signaling function: higher fares motivate additional drivers to enter the busy area while encouraging price-sensitive riders to wait or choose public transit. Critics, by contrast, contend that raising prices during emergencies or severe weather feels exploitative and erodes consumer trust. Balancing algorithmic efficiency with perceived fairness therefore remains a central challenge for modern service platforms.
